title: Every soul tastes death
hookLine: every soul shall taste death, and the world is the enjoyment of delusion (3:185)

lines: BAD NEWS IN THE FAMILY CHAT.
cards: A phone buzzes with bad news: a friend's grandfather has died. In the family chat come prayers for mercy, and then one line in Arabic. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt.

Every soul will taste death. To an outsider it can sound blunt, even cold, to send to a grieving family. To the people sending it, it's said gently: this road is everyone's road, and he did not walk it alone.

teach.b: Al 'Imran 185, in Pickthall's words, begins: "Every soul will taste of death." The same sentence appears in 21:35 and 29:57 as well; it's a line the Qur'an returns to. Notice the verb.
Not every soul will die, but every soul will taste death. Dha'iqa, from dhaqa, to taste.

Tasting is personal: nobody can taste something for you. And a taste is brief; it isn't the whole meal. Some readers hear a quiet hint in that: death is something the soul goes through, not where it ends.
The verse goes on: you'll be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever is drawn away from the Fire and brought into the Garden has truly won.
It ends, again in Pickthall's words: "The life of this world is but comfort of illusion." The Arabic is mata' al-ghurur.
Mata' is provision, things you use for a while, like supplies for a trip. Ghurur is deception, the kind that flatters you into forgetting. The world isn't called evil here.
It's called useful, and easy to be fooled by. A hadith in Tirmidhi tells people to remember often the destroyer of pleasures, meaning death.
Another, in Bukhari, says: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through.

teach.h: EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.
teach.b: The point isn't gloom. Travelers enjoy the road. They just don't forget where they're going.

how: Muslims recite 'every soul will taste death' at funerals, in condolences and in sermons, and it is sometimes carved on gravestones; remembering death is encouraged as a way to live with purpose, not in fear.

o: fearing death every day of your life
tasting: brief, personal, not the whole meal
dying: the soul's final end, once for all

games.q: every soul tastes death — tap the pairs.
p: how to be in this world

s: the line appears only once in the Qur'an
the verse calls the world evil
it calls it mata', provision, and easy to be fooled by.
a hadith tells people to remember death often
Tirmidhi reports: remember often the destroyer of pleasures.

games.q: the hadith says to be in this world in a certain way. which one?
o: as a king in his palace.
as a stranger, or a traveler passing through.
as a monk who owns nothing.
games.why: a stranger or a traveler (Bukhari): someone who uses the road and enjoys it, but doesn't forget where they're going.

practice: This one is gentle; if you're grieving right now, just breathe and skip ahead. Otherwise, sit comfortably and think, calmly, like a traveler checking the ticket, that your life has an end whose date you don't know.
Then ask: if this were a trip, what am I carrying that I won't need, and what am I forgetting to pack?

wordCard.voice: Dha'iqa, tasting: brief, and personal, not the whole meal. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt, from 3:185, and twice more in the Qur'an. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: every soul will taste death (3:185; also 21:35, 29:57).

carryVoice: Your line: every soul tastes it. Nobody walks this road alone, not even for a moment. Go gently today.

sources.q: Every soul will taste of death.
The life of this world is but comfort of illusion.
